name: Hee Bermiok
tagline: Farm homestays facing Kanchenjunga on the Pelling–Dentam road
meta_description: Hee Bermiok, West Sikkim: farm homestays with Kanchenjunga views on the Pelling–Dentam road. Cardamom farms, Limboo culture, costs and how to reach.
summary: Hee Bermiok is a farming village at roughly 1,900 m in Sikkim's Gyalshing district, on the road west from Pelling towards Dentam. Stay in a family homestay for clear Kanchenjunga dawns, organic farm walks among cardamom and alder, Limboo and Lepcha village life and dark night skies, at about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with meals.

local_story.title: Cardamom, alder and the people of the west
paras: Hee Bermiok has no famous monastery or battle, and we will not invent one. The double name is usually explained as joining two neighbouring settlements, Hee and Bermiok, and its story is the story of western Sikkim's farming people. Limboo families, whose homeland of Limbuwan ran across both sides of the Singalila ridge, and Lepcha families, the oldest people of Sikkim, farmed these slopes before the Namgyal dynasty was founded at Yuksom in 1642. Under the Chogyals the west was the kingdom's heartland, and in the late 1780s Gorkha armies from Nepal overran it before the border was restored in 1817.

From the late nineteenth century, especially after John Claude White became the first British Political Officer in Sikkim in 1889, Nepali-speaking farmers settled across western Sikkim and the village took on the mixed character it has today. Over the twentieth century, large cardamom grown under Himalayan alder trees became the main cash crop here, as across the state; Sikkim is India's largest producer. In 2003 the Limboo and Tamang communities were recognised as Scheduled Tribes in Sikkim, and in 2016 the state was declared fully organic, so Hee Bermiok's farms grow without chemical fertilisers or pesticides.

Above it all stands Kanchenjunga, 8,586 m, which much of Sikkim regards as a guardian deity. Each year at Pang Lhabsol, in August or September, monasteries honour the mountain with masked dances, and Lepcha tradition holds Kanchenjunga as the sacred source of their people. Homestays came to Hee Bermiok in recent decades, as Sikkim encouraged rural tourism, and families began hosting travellers who wanted the Pelling view without Pelling's hotels. It remains a farming village first.

did_you_know: The Limboo and Tamang communities were added to Sikkim's list of Scheduled Tribes in 2003, joining the Bhutia and Lepcha.
Sikkim's large cardamom is usually grown under Himalayan alder (Alnus nepalensis), a nitrogen-fixing tree that shades the plants and feeds the soil.
Pang Lhabsol, on the 15th day of the seventh Tibetan month (August–September), honours Kanchenjunga as Sikkim's guardian deity with masked warrior dances.
intro: Hee Bermiok is a working farm village on the road west from Pelling towards Dentam, spread over north-facing slopes at roughly 1,900 m. Its reason for being on a traveller's map is simple: family homestays with rooms that look straight across to the Kanchenjunga range, at village prices. Mornings start with the mountain turning pink, days go to farm walks among cardamom, alder, maize and kitchen gardens, and evenings are spent by the hearth with home-cooked food. The sky at night, far from town lights, is full of stars.

We suggest Hee Bermiok for couples and families who find Pelling too busy but do not want to travel as far as Uttarey. It is roughly an hour from Pelling by road, so you can still visit Pemayangtse and Rabdentse for the day. Homestays cost about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast. Come from mid-October to December for the clearest views, or in spring for flowers. Indians need no permit; foreign nationals need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, so check current status before you travel.
facts: Patchy; ask your host which network works best

highlights.title: Kanchenjunga across the valley
highlights.text: Many Hee Bermiok homestays face north to the Kanchenjunga range. From mid-October to December most dawns are clear, and you can watch the snow turn pink, gold and white from your room with a cup of tea. Ask for a north-facing room when you book.

highlights.title: Organic farm walks
highlights.text: Walk the village with your host through plots of large cardamom under alder trees, maize, millet, kitchen gardens and fruit trees. Sikkim has been fully organic since 2016, and families here can explain how they manage without chemical fertilisers or pesticides.

highlights.title: Limboo and Lepcha village life
highlights.text: Hee Bermiok's families include Limboo, Lepcha and Nepali-speaking households. Ask your hosts about their festivals, food and language; in Limboo homes you may hear of the Mundhum, the community's oral scripture, and drink tongba, millet beer in a bamboo mug.

highlights.title: Dark night skies
highlights.text: Far from town lights, Hee Bermiok gets properly dark on clear nights from October to April. Step outside after dinner and the Milky Way is often visible, with Kanchenjunga's snow faintly lit by starlight or moonlight. Bring a warm jacket and a red torch.

highlights.title: A quieter base for Pelling
highlights.text: Pemayangtse Monastery, the Rabdentse ruins and Sanga Choeling are about an hour away by car. Stay in Hee Bermiok for village quiet and lower prices, take a day car for the Pelling sights, and come back to a farmhouse dinner.

how_to_reach.text: Take a morning shared jeep from Siliguri to Gyalshing or Pelling (about 5–6 h, ₹450–600 a seat). From Gyalshing, jeeps heading west towards Dentam and Uttarey can drop you at Hee Bermiok for roughly ₹70–120; ask the driver and your host where to get off. Most leave in the morning and around midday.

From Pelling a small car takes about an hour and costs roughly ₹1,500–2,200 one way. From NJP or Bagdogra expect about ₹6,000–7,500 and 6–7 hours via Jorethang and Gyalshing. Fares are indicative; agree the price before you set off and check current road status in the monsoon.

where_to_stay: Hee Bermiok has a cluster of family homestays spread across the village, most with a few rooms, shared meals and dinner and breakfast included at roughly ₹1,500–2,500 per person. Some have newer guest rooms with attached bathrooms and geysers, others are simpler rooms in the family house; ask which you are getting. Choose a north-facing room for the Kanchenjunga view. Book ahead for October, November and the Puja and Diwali weeks. If the village is full, Pelling, about an hour away, has budget hotels such as Hotel Garuda in Upper Pelling.
tips: Ask for a north-facing room, because the Kanchenjunga view is the main reason to stay in Hee Bermiok.
Tell the jeep driver your homestay's name, since houses are spread out and there is no single village stop.
Draw cash in Gyalshing or Pelling before you arrive, as there are no reliable ATMs in the village.
Pack a warm layer and a torch; nights are cold and paths between houses are unlit.
Ask before walking into cardamom plots or picking fruit, since all the farmland is private.

experiences.title: Kanchenjunga sunrise from a Hee Bermiok farm
experiences.summary: Wake before dawn in your Hee Bermiok homestay and watch the Kanchenjunga range turn pink, gold and white across the valleys. No ticket, no crowd, no drive: just a farmhouse balcony, a cup of tea and Sikkim's guardian mountain in the first light.
body: Kanchenjunga, 8,586 m, is the third-highest mountain on earth and, for many in Sikkim, a guardian deity. Its name is usually read in Tibetan as the five treasures of the great snow, for its five summits. From Hee Bermiok you see the main massif and its neighbours as a long white wall above the forested ridges of West Sikkim. Unlike Pelling, where hotel roofs fill with people at dawn, here you usually share the view only with your hosts and their cows.

Set an alarm for about 30 minutes before sunrise, around 5.15 am in October and closer to 5.45 am in December. The highest summits catch the light first, turning pink, then orange, then white as the sun climbs. The show lasts 15–20 minutes, and by 9 or 10 am cloud often rises from the valleys. Most mornings from mid-October to December are clear; March and April are good but hazier, and the monsoon usually hides the range.

A north-facing balcony or yard is all you need, so ask for one when you book. If yours faces the wrong way, your host can show you a field edge nearby. Bring a warm layer, a cap and a flask, since dawn can be close to freezing in December. For photographs, a short telephoto lens pulls the peaks in, and a wider shot that includes the farm terraces and prayer flags tells the story better.

faqs.q: Can we see Kanchenjunga from Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: Yes. On clear days the Kanchenjunga range is visible to the north from much of the village, and many homestays have north-facing rooms or balconies. Your best chances are at dawn from mid-October to December, with a second window in March and early April. From June to September the peaks are usually hidden by monsoon cloud.

faqs.q: Is the view from Hee Bermiok as good as from Pelling?
faqs.a: It is similar: both look north across West Sikkim to the same range. Pelling sits slightly higher with more open ridge-top viewpoints, while Hee Bermiok gives you a quieter, farm-framed view without crowds. If you stay in either with a north-facing room on a clear morning, you will not feel short-changed.

faqs.q: What time should we wake up for the sunrise?
faqs.a: About 30 minutes before sunrise: around 5.15 am in October and 5.45 am in December. Check the exact sunrise time on your phone the evening before. The first light on the summits comes 15–20 minutes before the sun appears over the eastern hills, so be in place early.

experiences.title: Organic farm walk among cardamom and alder
experiences.summary: Walk through Hee Bermiok's terraces with a member of your host family to see how an organic Sikkim farm works: large cardamom under alder, maize and millet, kitchen gardens, cattle and compost. You come back knowing what was on your dinner plate and how it got there.
body: Sikkim was declared India's first fully organic state in January 2016, after a gradual phase-out of chemical fertilisers and pesticides. In a village like Hee Bermiok that policy is visible in small things: compost heaps, cow-dung manure carried to the fields, mixed planting, and kitchen gardens of beans, squash, mustard greens and chillies. Ask your host how the change affected yields and prices; the answers are honest and often mixed, and they tell you more than any brochure.

The main cash crop is large cardamom, grown in damp plots shaded by Himalayan alder, a fast-growing tree that fixes nitrogen and improves the soil. The pods grow in red clusters at the base of the plants and are harvested from about August to November, then dried over wood fires in bhatti kilns. Around the cardamom you will see maize and finger millet on the terraces, fruit trees such as oranges and guava lower down, and cattle kept for milk, manure and churpi cheese.

Go mid-morning after breakfast and allow two hours. Most homestays will send a family member with you for no fixed fee; a tip of ₹200–300 is a kind thank-you. Walk only where you are led, never pick anything without asking, and keep out of the cardamom plots unless invited, since the plants are fragile. Wear shoes with grip for terrace paths. If you want to buy cardamom, churpi or seasonal produce, ask your host; it supports the family directly.

faqs.q: Is everything grown in Hee Bermiok organic?
faqs.a: Sikkim was declared a fully organic state in 2016, and chemical fertilisers and pesticides are restricted across the state, so village farms like those in Hee Bermiok grow without them. Farmers use compost, manure and mixed planting. Ask your host how they manage pests and soil; practices vary from family to family.

faqs.q: When is the best time for a farm walk?
faqs.a: September to November is best: cardamom harvest and drying, maize and millet coming in, and clear skies. Spring, from March to April, shows planting and flowering. Winter is quieter on the farms but still pleasant. The monsoon months are green but muddy, with leeches on the paths.

faqs.q: Can we buy farm produce from our hosts?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Ask your host whether they have cardamom, churpi, pickles or seasonal fruit to sell. Prices follow local markets and are fair; cardamom in particular is not cheap. Buying directly is one of the best ways to support the family you stay with. Carry small notes, as change can be scarce.

experiences.title: Limboo kitchen evening and tongba by the fire
experiences.summary: If your host family is Limboo, ask to spend the evening by their hearth learning about Limboo food, language and festivals over a bamboo mug of tongba. Even in non-Limboo homes, a farm kitchen evening is the best way to understand who lives in Hee Bermiok and how.
body: The Limboo, also written Limbu, are one of the oldest peoples of the eastern Himalaya, with a homeland, Limbuwan, that ran across both sides of the Singalila ridge into what is now eastern Nepal. They have their own language, their own script, often called Sirijunga after an eighteenth-century scholar who championed it, and an oral scripture, the Mundhum, recited by their priests at births, weddings and funerals. In 2003 the Limboo were recognised as a Scheduled Tribe in Sikkim.

Tongba is the drink most associated with the Limboo: fermented finger millet packed into a tall bamboo or wooden vessel, topped up with hot water and sipped through a bamboo straw. The water is refilled several times as the evening goes on. Food may include kinema, fermented soybean, gundruk greens, local rice, pork or chicken on festival days, and chilli relishes. Ask about the Chyabrung, the two-sided drum played in Limboo dances, and whether anyone in the house still plays.

Hee Bermiok's homestays are run by families of several communities, not only Limboo, so ask when you book and do not assume. Whoever your hosts are, the evening by the kitchen fire is where you learn the most, about festivals, crops, children who have moved to Gangtok or Bengaluru, and how life has changed since the road came. Drink tongba slowly, as it is stronger than it tastes, and it is fine to say no. Offer to help wash up.

faqs.q: What is tongba?
faqs.a: Tongba is a traditional Limboo drink of fermented finger millet packed into a tall bamboo or wooden vessel, topped up with hot water and sipped through a bamboo straw. The vessel is refilled with hot water several times. It is mildly alcoholic but adds up over an evening, so drink slowly and skip it if you are unwell or on medication.

faqs.q: Are all homestays in Hee Bermiok run by Limboo families?
faqs.a: No. The village has Limboo, Lepcha and Nepali-speaking families of several communities. If you are particularly interested in Limboo culture, ask when you book whether the host family is Limboo. Every family has its own food and festival stories, so a kitchen evening is worthwhile whoever you stay with.

faqs.q: What should we bring for our homestay hosts?
faqs.a: A small gift is welcome but never expected: tea, sweets or fruit from the plains, or something from your home town. Avoid alcohol unless you know the family drinks. Offer to help in the kitchen or wash up, ask before taking photographs, and take your rubbish with you when you leave.

experiences.title: Stargazing over the Kanchenjunga ridges
experiences.image_query: Milky Way Himalaya night sky Sikkim
experiences.summary: On clear, moonless nights from October to March, Hee Bermiok gets properly dark. Step out after dinner, let your eyes adjust for 15 minutes and look for the Milky Way, Orion and the Pleiades above the faint white line of the Kanchenjunga range.
body: At roughly 1,900 m and far from any large town, Hee Bermiok has little light pollution, and the dry, clear air of autumn and winter makes for sharp skies. On a moonless night the Milky Way is often visible as a pale band across the sky, especially in October and November, when it arcs overhead in the early evening. In winter, Orion rises in the east after dinner, with the Pleiades above it. If the moon is up, the snow of Kanchenjunga glows faintly to the north, which is a sight of its own.

Plan around the moon. The best nights are within a few days either side of the new moon; check a moon calendar before you book. Step outside about 8 pm, switch off your phone screen or use a red torch, and give your eyes 15 minutes to adjust. A north- or east-facing yard away from the house lights works best. Binoculars help with star clusters, and a phone app can name what you see.

Dress for cold. From November to February night temperatures at this height can fall to near freezing, so wear a down jacket, cap and gloves and take a blanket to sit on. Stay on familiar ground near your homestay, since paths are unlit and terraces drop away sharply. For photographs, use a tripod, a wide lens and exposures of 15–20 seconds. Cloud can roll in quickly, so make the most of clear spells.

faqs.q: When is the best time for stargazing in Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: October to March, on clear nights within a few days of the new moon. October and November show the Milky Way well in the early evening; December to February bring crisp skies and winter constellations such as Orion. The monsoon, from June to September, is usually cloudy, and a full moon washes out fainter stars.

faqs.q: Do we need a telescope?
faqs.a: No. The naked eye shows the Milky Way, constellations and bright planets on a dark night. Binoculars add star clusters and the moon's craters. A phone app helps you name stars and planets. If you photograph the sky, bring a tripod and a camera or phone with a long-exposure night mode.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk around the village at night?
faqs.a: The village is safe, but paths are unlit and terraces drop steeply, so stay near your homestay in a spot you saw in daylight. Use a red torch to keep your night vision, wear shoes with grip and keep children close. Tell your hosts you are going outside, and watch for dogs.

faqs.q: Is Hee Bermiok worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want a quiet farm homestay with a Kanchenjunga view and no crowds. Hee Bermiok has no headline sight, but it gives you clear dawns, organic farm walks, village kitchens and dark night skies, about an hour from Pelling's monasteries. One or two nights suit most people; come between mid-October and April.

faqs.q: How far is Hee Bermiok from Pelling?
faqs.a: It is on the road west from Pelling towards Dentam, roughly an hour by car. A reserved car costs about ₹1,500–2,200 one way. By shared jeep, go to Gyalshing and take a jeep heading towards Dentam or Uttarey, asking to be dropped at Hee Bermiok. Fares and timings are indicative, so confirm locally.

faqs.q: How do we reach Hee Bermiok from NJP?
faqs.a: Take a morning shared jeep from Siliguri to Gyalshing or Pelling (about 5–6 h, ₹450–600 a seat), then a jeep from Gyalshing towards Dentam, or a car from Pelling. A reserved car from NJP or Bagdogra costs about ₹6,000–7,500 and takes 6–7 hours. Check current road status in the monsoon.

faqs.q: Should we stay in Pelling or Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: Stay in Pelling if you want hotels, restaurants and the monasteries on your doorstep; stay in Hee Bermiok for village quiet, farm food and lower prices with a similar mountain view. Many travellers do both: one or two nights in Pelling for sightseeing, then one or two in Hee Bermiok to slow down.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: Mid-October to December brings the clearest Kanchenjunga views and dry days. March and April are pleasant, with spring flowers and some haze. January and February are clear but cold at night. June to September is wet, with leeches, landslide risk and hidden mountains, so most people avoid it.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit for Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: Indian citizens do not need a permit. Foreign nationals need the Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, available online or at entry points such as Rangpo and Melli, which covers Hee Bermiok and the rest of West Sikkim. Rules change from time to time, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Hee Bermiok good for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes. Children usually love the farm animals, the fields and the space to run, and homestay food is simple and filling. Watch them near terrace edges and on unlit paths after dark. Pack warm clothes for the evenings, a torch and some snacks, and ask about hot water and attached bathrooms when you book.

faqs.q: How many days should we spend in Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: One night gives you a dawn view and a farm walk; two nights add a stargazing evening, a slow day and a second chance at the mountain if the first morning is cloudy. Combine it with Pelling for sightseeing, or continue west to Dentam and Uttarey for a longer village trail.

faqs.q: How much does a stay in Hee Bermiok cost?
faqs.a: A homestay costs roughly ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with dinner and breakfast. Add about ₹1,500–2,200 for a car from Pelling, or ₹70–120 for a shared jeep seat from Gyalshing, plus small sums for tea, snacks and tips. A day car for Pelling's sights costs about ₹2,500–3,500. Figures are indicative for 2025–26.
